title: Part 1
text: Here is a puzzle. Parasites usually do best when their hosts stay alive and healthy. So why would Ribeiroia cripple its frog?

title: Part 2
text: When the tadpole finishes its metamorphosis and crawls onto land, it is badly damaged.
nxt: A normal frog relies on powerful hind legs to leap away from danger, dive into water, and catch fast insects.

nxt: A frog with tangled legs cannot jump properly. Every attempt ends in clumsy flailing, and even moving a few inches takes huge effort.

title: Part 3
text: This is the part that makes biologists shiver. The deformity may not be a side effect that happens to hurt the frog.
nxt: Researchers argue that it is part of what makes the whole plan work. Remember, the worm has no eyes and no brain. It plans nothing.

title: Part 4
text: Now look at the sky. A heron, an egret, or a hunting duck glides above the reeds. Waterbirds like these are final hosts for the parasite.
nxt: Only inside a bird's gut can the adult worm mature and reproduce. But a microscopic worm in a pond cannot simply fly up and infect a bird.

title: Part 5
text: Here is the sinister genius. The parasite builds a bridge, and the bridge is predation.
nxt: A healthy, agile frog spots the heron, leaps into deep water, and escapes. A crippled frog is a sitting duck on the shoreline.

title: Part 6
text: When a heron spots a deformed frog thrashing in the shallows, its spear-like beak strikes downward and the bird swallows the frog whole.
nxt: The frog's life ends. But for the parasites encysted in its distorted legs, the plan has worked.

title: Part 7
text: In the bird's stomach, the cyst walls dissolve. The flatworms attach to the intestinal wall, mature into adults, and produce eggs.
nxt: The eggs leave the bird in its droppings.

title: Part 7

title: Part 8
text: The bird then flies on, perhaps for many miles, and drops them into new ponds and wetlands.
nxt: The eggs hatch into miracidia, which begin hunting for ramshorn snails. The circle is complete.

title: Part 9
text: Through evolution alone, a brainless flatworm has manipulated the body of a vertebrate to steer its own journey across the sky.
